status: Draft classroom materials; teacher approval required per lesson

weeks.title: What Is AI? Rules and Learning
course: Search is not the same as learning
lab: Predict one Quick, Draw! guess before it finishes.
Train two object categories in Teachable Machine without photographing people.
Run the small nearest-prototype Python notebook; change two training examples.
Record one misleading prediction and explain why it occurs.
homework: Implement the fixed thermostat rule and test it at 17°C, 19°C and 22°C.
Use a supplied trained ID3 component to learn from a simple heating decision log; plot predictions. You are not required to implement ID3 from scratch yet.
weeks.research: Compare fixed threshold and supplied learned classifier on a new heating CSV and explain any disagreement.

weeks.title: Supervised Learning: ID3
course: Entropy: how mixed is a group?
Information gain and a greedy tree
lab: Predict whether sky or wind will be the best first question.
Calculate the gain for every root feature.
Run a categorical ID3 notebook and compare its learned tree.
Remove one example and predict it as a held-out case.
homework: Compute the information gain of at least two feature tests.
Load the provided weather decisions, fit the supplied ID3 code and trace three unseen examples.
weeks.research: Test the learner on an unseen category and explain how your fallback behaves.

weeks.title: Unsupervised Learning: K-Means
course: No labels: a different learning problem
lab: Plot six delivery points on a grid.
Manually calculate the centre for one proposed cluster.
Open the K-Means visualisation; change the starting centres.
Run the supplied notebook and compare its final grouping to your guess.
homework: Calculate the centroid of three given locations.
Use the K-Means notebook to cluster new delivery addresses and produce a labelled scatterplot.
weeks.research: Find a point arrangement where K=2 produces a misleading grouping.

weeks.title: Revision: Supervised and Unsupervised Learning
lab: Label a few points with known categories.
Predict a new point with K=3 nearest neighbours.
Remove labels and group the points with K-Means.
Compare what each result answers, and inspect an ID3 classification trace.
homework: Explain which method serves each of the two needs.
Modify the lab KNN code to classify new points and compare K=1 vs K=3.
weeks.research: Investigate a dataset where the choice of K changes the KNN prediction.

weeks.title: Computer Vision: Images as Data
course: The picture is a grid of numbers
lab: Experiment with a tiny grayscale pixel grid.
Use an interactive filter to compare blur and edges.
Run the image notebook to convert pixels to black and white.
Explain which filter preserves the handwriting best.
homework: Apply a threshold to five pixel values.
Modify the supplied image-preprocessing notebook and show side-by-side images.
weeks.research: Implement a custom 3×3 edge kernel on a tiny matrix and show the result.

weeks.title: Perceptrons: A First Learning Neuron
course: A neuron computes a weighted sum
A perceptron can learn from errors
lab: Calculate a single neuron's weighted sum by hand.
Move weights in a browser neural-network visualiser.
Run a tiny perceptron on six labelled examples.
Find one observation that a straight-line boundary handles poorly.
homework: Compute neuron outputs for three inputs.
Modify two weights and a bias in the lab notebook to classify new examples.
weeks.research: Write one perceptron weight update and show how the boundary changes.

weeks.title: Neural Networks and Training
course: Why a network needs hidden layers
From input to output: forward pass
lab: Try XOR with no hidden layer and record the result.
Add hidden neurons in the visual playground.
Run the notebook and plot training loss over iterations.
Change the learning rate and compare convergence.
homework: Calculate one neuron activation and loss.
Change the hidden layer size in the supplied notebook and compare accuracy.
weeks.research: Compare two network sizes and explain overfitting risk using the same training data.

weeks.title: Revision: Computer Vision and Neural Networks
lab: Draw two variants of the same digit.
Inspect an 8×8 pixel representation.
Run the supplied classifier on held-out examples.
Explain one error and try a preprocessing change.
homework: Interpret the model's confusion table and compute accuracy.
Use the evaluation notebook to compare predictions before and after image preprocessing.
weeks.research: Build a small error gallery: three wrong predictions with possible causes.

weeks.title: Mid-Term Evaluation
lab: Choose a suitable algorithm for three real-life scenarios.
Repair a small classifier example by filling missing values.
Run predictions on a held-out set.
Explain a chosen decision in a short diagram.
homework: Prepare a one-page visual explanation of a model.
Correct a small notebook and add an honest evaluation table.
weeks.research: Compare two eligible algorithms and defend the choice using evaluation evidence.

weeks.title: Generative AI: GPT, Data and Society
lab: Inspect how a short sentence is tokenised.
Change the text-generation sampling setting in the visual explainer.
Compare two hypothetical recommendation feeds generated from different click histories.
Check three claims against independent references.
homework: Tokenise a short sentence and identify two risks of trusting its generated completion.
Build a table of three generated claims, their source evidence and a verdict.
weeks.research: Design a small evaluation rubric for harmful or misleading recommendations.

weeks.title: Software Engineering Techniques
course: From one long script to several components
lab: Run a project made of three small Python classes.
Change the behaviour of one class and check its outputs.
Use the accountless Git simulation to create and compare versions.
Demonstrate one test that catches an invalid measurement.
homework: Create a Sensor class with a method that returns a reading.
Add input validation and a classifier component, then test normal and missing data.
weeks.research: Add a fourth component and explain which other components it depends on.

weeks.title: FIICode I: Understanding the Challenge
course: Turn a problem into inputs and outputs
lab: Read the exact challenge rules and identify allowed inputs.
Inspect a small CSV without changing the provided answer column.
Choose a baseline and run it on held-out examples.
Write down the model's first score and one weakness.
homework: Write a one-paragraph problem statement and a data dictionary.
Deliver a runnable baseline notebook with a metric and a description of its input/output.
weeks.research: Compare two possible baselines and justify which is easier to maintain.

weeks.title: FIICode II: Implementing the Application
lab: Load an example input and validate its fields.
Connect the prepared model to a simple interface.
Test the main success path and one error path.
Save a working version before extending anything else.
homework: Expose a simple input and readable prediction.
Add one validation rule and three small tests.
weeks.research: Design a second output format, for example a report CSV with an explanation.

weeks.title: FIICode III: Improving and Testing
lab: Choose one reproducible failure case.
Make one model or input-processing change.
Compare results on the same held-out samples.
Write one brief test report and decide whether to keep the change.
homework: Record the baseline metric and two failed cases.
Implement one controlled change and explain its measured effect.
weeks.research: Run an ablation or a repeated evaluation to see whether the improvement is stable.

weeks.title: FIICode IV: Hackathon
course: Deliver something someone else can run
lab: Confirm the project works from a clean start.
Execute representative and edge test cases.
Present the demo with baseline/final scores.
Collect reviewer feedback and record next improvements.
homework: Submit a reproducible build or notebook with a README.
Provide a brief demo, validation evidence and an honest limitations section.
weeks.research: Attempt a suitable official competition extension or produce a full technical postmortem.
